title: Coast Guard Air Station Kodiak launches for Sailboat Taking on Water near Homer, Alaska
description: A Coast Guard MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter aircrew from Air Station Kodiak launched for a sailing vessel taking on water near Homer, Alaska, on July 19, 2016. U.S. Coast Guard video by Auxiliarist Tracey Mertens.
keywords: rescue swimmer, Air Station Kodiak, Coast Guard rescue, MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter, Coast Guard, Alaska

transcript.text: (dramatic piano music)
^- We received the SAR call at about 10:45
^of a fishing vessel taking on water
in the vicinity of Homer, Alaska.
We quickly deployed, and as we were on our way to the scene,
we continued to receive reports
of pumps failing one after another,
until they were down to bailing with buckets.
We arrived on scene,
I was lowered down to the water
and swam about 20 or 30 yards to the vessel.
(dramatic electronic music)
My primary job is to rescue someone when I get on scene,
is to inspect the health and well-being of the survivors.
In this case, there were no injuries,
so we then moved to checking out the vessel
to make sure that we could remain on it.
We inspected the cabin, which had approximately
two to three feet of water,
in the engine compartment,
which had roughly 4 1/2, five feet of water.
At that point we decided the vessel was riding well enough
that we could attempt to pump water out.
I was on that vessel for approximately two to three hours,
and this time we got the pump up and running.
We run it for about 15 to 20 minute increments
before securing it,
only to have to turn it back on when the cabin
would again fill with water.
Shortly after getting there,
a good samaritan showed up on scene
and was able to tie a line off to the vessel,
and begin towing it towards shore.
Then another 20 or 30 minutes later,
another good samaritan vessel was able to show up
with another salvage pump,
^which we were also able to get running.
^- We remained on scene in orbit to provide coverage
^to the vessel in case they ended up taking on water again,
^and we needed to get the crew
^and the rescue swimmer off the boat.
^We constantly do these kind of things just to make sure
^everything goes smoothly and no further damage comes to
^either the boat, or to the crew themselves.
(dramatic electronic music)
